papers.title_in_file: Quantum Neuron Selection: Finding High Performing Subnetworks With Quantum Algorithms
papers.what_it_is: A short conceptual GECCO companion paper that formulates neural-network neuron selection for quantum algorithms and proposes three local variants, with no experiments.

assertions.value: The author proposes three approaches for local quantum neuron selection (Quantum Edge-Popup, Layerwise Knowledge Distillation, and NK Echo State Networks) and states that they are tractable for current quantum systems.
quotes: Nevertheless, we introduce several approaches for performing local quantum neuron selection that are tractable for current quantum systems.
The first is Quantum Edge-Popup, a variational method that embeds parameterized quantum circuits into classical neural networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim of tractability; the paper reports no simulation, hardware run or accuracy result.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper contains no experiment, so tractability is asserted, not measured.

assertions.value: The author states that, because of the scale of deep neural networks and the fragility of current quantum systems, pure quantum neuron selection will require significant advances in both hardware and software.
quotes: Due to the scale of deep neural networks and the fragility of current quantum systems, pure quantum neuron selection will require significant advances in both hardware and software.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit on global quantum neuron selection, Section 4, p.5.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing other work, that in general variational and annealing algorithms do not have computational complexity guarantees over classical methods.
quotes: In general, variational and annealing algorithms do not have computational complexity guarantees over classical methods [1].
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited statement attributed to lecture notes (reference 1), not shown in the paper.

assertions.value: The author states that there is no efficient classical algorithm for finding the best subnetwork in a given network, while several works have shown that large networks contain subnetworks that perform as well as fully trained networks.
quotes: However, there is no efficient classical algorithm for finding the best subnetwork in a given network.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the state of the field with no proof or experiment in the paper.

papers.title_in_file: Component Based Quantum Machine Learning Explainability
papers.what_it_is: A student-style paper adapting SHAP and ALE, through a state-fidelity pseudo model, to explain the feature map, ansatz and quantum kernel of a VQC and a QSVC on the Pima Indians Diabetes data.

assertions.value: The authors state that applying explainability techniques to the core components of QML algorithms, rather than to the whole model, gives insights into feature and parameter importance that would otherwise be hidden.
quotes: The answer: Yes. The component based explainability techniques developed in this project clearly show the benefits of using these techniques, as well as the need.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own conclusion from qualitative plots on one dataset, with no baseline explainer compared quantitatively.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper shows plots for one dataset on a simulator and does not measure how much a whole-model explainer misses.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the QSVC quantum kernel on the Pima Indians Diabetes data, 156 components capture 99% of the variance, and that a surrogate model of the QSVC decision function reached a 0.98 R2 score.
quotes: which shows that 156 components capture 99% of the variance in the data, which implies a high effective dimensionality for the kernel
obtained a 0.98 R2 score, so 98% replication of results
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulated run on one dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study covers the VQC and QSVC hybrid algorithms only, on the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset, with 8 features encoded on 8 qubits, using classical data encoded by a feature map.
quotes: This paper focused on the VQC and QSVC algorithms, which are both quantum-classical hybrid algorithms.
As the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset has 8 features, this means that 8 qubits are needed when encoding.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope, Sections II.A and II.C.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion also refers to the limited dataset size and to training on a simulator, so no hardware result is reported.

assertions.value: The authors claim that their paper is the first to apply explainability techniques to the core parts of QML algorithms rather than to the algorithm as a whole.
quotes: This paper is the first to apply techniques to the core parts of QML algorithms, rather than viewing QML algorithms as monolithic entities and applying explainability techniques to the algorithm as a whole.
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority claim by the authors, checked only against five prior papers they review.

papers.title_in_file: Partitioned-Constraint QAOA (PC-QAOA): Structural State Preparation and Penalty Enforcement for Quantum Optimization
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv 2508.02590 v2 (18 May 2026). Its title differs from the earlier title in the file name (Learning Feasible Quantum States ...), but the arXiv identifier is the same, so I treated it as the same paper and extracted it.
papers.what_it_is: A QAOA variant that enforces some constraints structurally through feasible-state preparation and a Grover mixer and the rest through penalties, tested by exact simulation on small random instances.

assertions.value: The authors report, from exact statevector simulation on 413 completed instances, that PC-QAOA reaches mean P(feas) = 0.912 against 0.420 for penalty-based QAOA at p = 1, and mean P(opt) = 0.242 against 0.077.
assertions.anchor: Section VII Conclusion and Future Work, p.14; Section VI.C, p.10
quotes: Across 413 completed instances spanning multiple constraint families, PC-QAOA substantially improves feasibility and solution quality at shallow depth relative to penalty-based QAOA
PC-QAOA achieves mean P (feas) = 0.912 vs. 0.420 at p = 1 and mean P (opt) = 0.242 vs. 0.077 compared to PenaltyQAOA.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulation study on small random instances.
assertions.reader_inference: Only 413 of 500 PC-QAOA runs and 316 of 500 PenaltyQAOA runs completed, so the two methods are not compared on identical instance sets.

assertions.value: The paper proves that gadgets for constraints with pairwise disjoint supports compose exactly, so the joint feasible superposition is a tensor product prepared in parallel.
assertions.anchor: Section IV Proposition IV.1, p.4; Abstract
quotes: We show that constraints with disjoint support can be prepared in parallel with little error accumulation.
The following proposition formalizes when gadgets compose without conflict.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proposition IV.1 and its proof, with Corollary IV.2 for approximate gadgets, Section IV, p.4-6.

assertions.value: The authors state that all simulations are exact statevector runs on classical hardware and that the experiments do not aim to demonstrate quantum advantage over classical methods.
quotes: All simulations use PennyLane [38] with JAX and qjit just-in-time compilation, and are run on classical hardware via exact statevector simulation.
These experiments do not aim to demonstrate quantum advantage over classical methods, which requires problem sizes well beyond current hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope, Section VI.A, p.9.

assertions.value: The authors state that the primary limitation of variational constraint gadgets is exponential dependence on constraint support size, and that scalability to large-support constraints limits the structural encoding.
assertions.anchor: Section IV.D, p.6; Section VII, p.14
quotes: The primary limitation of VCGs is the exponential dependence on constraint support size.
A key limitation of PC-QAOA's structural encoding component is its scalability to large-support constraints.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit, Sections IV.D and VII.

papers.what_it_is: A short proceedings report on supercomputer simulations of QAOA, approximate quantum annealing and VQE (Heisenberg model) with the JUQCS simulator.

assertions.value: The authors report from simulation of a tail assignment problem that the QAOA scales much better than random guessing but needs significant computational resources, and that approximate quantum annealing reaches the same promising scaling with much less computation.
quotes: We find that the QAOA scales much better to larger problems than random guessing, but requires significant computational resources.
In contrast, a coarsely discretised version of quantum annealing called approximate quantum annealing (AQA) can reach the same promising scaling behaviour using much less computational resources.
Both QAOA and AQA obtain better success probabilities than can be found by random guessing
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result; the text says two instances per problem size were simulated.
assertions.reader_inference: The scaling is still exponential, and the QAOA parameters were initialised from AQA results.

assertions.value: The authors report reasonable ground state energies for the Heisenberg model with the VQE when suitable initial states and parameters are used, and state that random initialisation is not a suitable strategy.
quotes: For the VQE, we find reasonable results in approximating the ground state energy of the Heisenberg model when suitable choices of initial states and parameters are used.
It is crucial to have a good combination of ansatz and initial parameters to have a reasonable chance of finding the ground state energy.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result for one model and one ansatz.

assertions.value: The authors state that at the largest problem size, N = 40 qubits, the full QAOA optimisation reached the cap of 200 simulator calls and did not converge.
assertions.anchor: Section 3.4 Results, p.8; Section 5 Conclusions, p.11
quotes: Here, the maximum number of 200 JUQCS-calls (and thus the limit of the computational budget allocated for this job) was reached.
However, due to tremendous computational resources required for simulations with N = 40 qubits, it was not possible to reach convergence for the largest problem size.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit, Section 3.4 and Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors report that quasi-dynamical evolution on isotropic Heisenberg rings of lengths 7 to 12 found a better energy fidelity than a Neel start or the best of random restarts, and state that the simple ansatz choice may not always converge to the ground state energy.
quotes: We perform the quasi-dynamical evolution on isotropic rings of lengths 7 to 12.
We observe that the quasi-dynamical evolution can find a better energy fidelity.
While it improves the results for the cases we tested, such an elementary choice may not always converge to the ground state energy.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result on small rings, shown in a figure only.
assertions.reader_inference: The size of the improvement is in Figure 5(b) and is not stated in the text.

papers.title_in_file: Variational Quantum Eigensolver for Classification in Credit Sales Risk
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study that classifies credit-sales customers into low and high risk with a VQE-trained ansatz and a SWAP-test distance, using a small data set from a Polish pharmaceutical wholesaler.

assertions.value: The authors report 100% classification efficiency for the tuned circuit variant (B) with a two-layer circuit, after the classification thresholds were selected, on credit-sales data from a Polish pharmaceutical wholesaler covering a period in 2003.
quotes: the parameters of the classification threshold were also properly selected, what provided a high, 100%, classification efficiency (No. 7 and 11, Table 4) by only two-layer circuit
Training data utilized in this work was gained from one of Polish pharmaceutical wholesalers and concerns some period of time in 2003.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one small data set, with thresholds tuned by hand.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper tunes the acceptance thresholds and repeats VQE training, and it describes no held-out test set, so the 100% is a tuned fit and not a generalization estimate.

assertions.value: The authors report that some classical classifiers also reached 100.0 % fit to the training data, using more complex models such as SVM with a polynomial kernel.
assertions.anchor: Section 3.4 Accuracy of classical classifiers, p.13; Section 6, p.25
quotes: It may be observed that some classifiers reached 100.0 % fit to our training data. However, these cases present complex models with the polynomial kernel functions.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one small data set, reported in Table 3.
assertions.reader_inference: Classical and quantum models reach the same fit on this data, so the data does not separate them on accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study uses one customer-risk data set with seven decision variables padded to eight and encoded on three qubits, and that calculations and simulations were done in Python.
quotes: All calculations, simulations, plots, and comparisons were implemented and conduced in the Python language environment.
In the analyzed problem, the eight input features require the use of three qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope and setup, Abstract and Section 5.2, p.22.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says the circuit could run on NISQ devices, but the paper reports no hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that their solution is compact and needs only a logarithmically increasing number of qubits.
quotes: The elaborated solution is compact and requires only logarithmically increasing number of qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about qubit count that follows from amplitude encoding; no resource-comparison result is given.

papers.title_in_file: LEARNING THE COMPLEXITY OF WEAKLY NOISY QUANTUM STATES
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv 2303.17813 v4 (21 May 2025, ICLR 2025). Its title differs from the earlier title in the file name (Complexity analysis of weakly noisy quantum states via quantum machine learning), but the arXiv identifier matches the record year 2025, so I treated it as the same paper and extracted it.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections 1 to 7 (introduction, definitions, problem statement, algorithm, theorems 1 to 4 statements and proof outline, numerical simulations, conclusion), and Appendices B and C. I did not read the proofs in Appendices G to J line by line.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper presenting a classical-shadow and Bayesian-optimization learning algorithm that predicts a limited-structure circuit complexity of weakly noisy quantum states, with a sample-complexity lower bound and a small Ising-model simulation.

assertions.value: The paper proves, in its efficiency theorem and its sample lower-bound theorem, that its learning algorithm, which uses the classical shadow of the state, predicts the limited-structure complexity of weakly noisy states with polynomial classical processing time, and that its sample complexity is optimal (abstract) or nearly optimal (body) in the noisy circuit depth.
quotes: We present an efficient learning algorithm, that leverages the classical shadow representation of target quantum states, to predict the circuit complexity of weakly noisy quantum states.
Our algorithm is proved to be optimal in terms of sample complexity accompanied with polynomial classical processing time.
and our learning algorithm is nearly-optimal in terms of the circuit depth
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2 (efficiency) and Theorem 3 (sample lower bound), Section 5, pp.7-8, with proofs in the appendices.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says optimal and the body says nearly-optimal. The guarantee holds for the limited-structure complexity under a fixed circuit architecture, not for general state complexity.

assertions.value: The paper restricts attention to weakly noisy quantum states, produced by shallow circuits with a small noise rate, under a general gate-independent and time-invariant noise channel.
quotes: Here, we focus primarily on the complexity of weakly noisy quantum states to avoid the anticoncentration property
a general noise channel which is both gate-independent and time-invariant, such as the local-depolarizing channel, the global-depolarizing channel, the bit-flip channel and other common noise models.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope and definitions, Section 1 and Definition 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the work is essentially theoretical research, that the algorithm has not yet been tested on practical quantum platforms, and that gate-dependent noise is left as an open question.
assertions.anchor: Appendix B and Appendix C, p.16-17
quotes: This work is essentially a theoretical research, and the algorithm has not yet been explicitly tested on these practical platforms.
We leave an open question of how to depict the gate-dependent noise, which usually happens in larger, more complex quantum architectures.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limits, Appendix B and Appendix C.

assertions.value: The authors report from numerical simulation of a transverse-field Ising model under local depolarizing noise that the estimated complexity lower bound of weakly noisy states may not grow with circuit depth, and that shallower noisy states had a higher lower bound.
quotes: This result highlights weakly noisy quantum state complexity lower bound may not grow with the circuit depth, which is dramatically different to that of pure states.
where a shallower circuit depth weakly noisy states possess higher state complexity lower bound.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation on a small lattice with a lower-bound estimate from a restricted architecture.
assertions.reader_inference: The figures hold the numbers. The text gives only the qualitative trend, and the bound is for the limited-structure complexity.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum convolutional neural network for predicting nuclear charge radii
papers.what_it_is: A noiseless-simulation study that replaces the last 2x2 convolutional filter of a CNN with a four-qubit variational quantum filter to predict nuclear charge radii, compared with the classical CNN.

assertions.value: The authors report that over 10 independent runs the mean full-set RMSE was 0.0091 fm for the classical CNN and 0.0071 fm for the QCNN, with standard deviations of 0.0007 fm and 0.0006 fm.
assertions.anchor: Section III Results and Discussion, p.6
quotes: Finally, to assess robustness against training randomness, each model was trained in 10 independent runs.
Across these runs, the mean RMSE values on the full set are 0.0091 fm for the CNN and 0.0071 fm for the QCNN, with standard deviations of 0.0007 fm and 0.0006 fm, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on one dataset in noiseless simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The gap is about three standard deviations of either model, but the paper gives no significance test.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the 27 nuclei measured after 2021, used as an extrapolation test set, the CNN and the QCNN reach overall RMSE values of 0.0167 fm and 0.0147 fm.
assertions.anchor: Section II p.5; Section III p.6
quotes: the 27 nuclei whose charge radii were measured after 2021 are selected as the extrapolation test set
The CNN and QCNN achieve overall RMSE values of 0.0167 fm and 0.0147 fm, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one small test set.

assertions.value: The authors state that the CNN and QCNN share the same input, trunk, pooling, fully connected layers and optimizer, that the dataset holds 1018 nuclei split 4:1 into training and validation sets, that the quantum filter has 12 trainable rotation parameters, and that the calculations use noiseless quantum-circuit simulations.
assertions.anchor: Section I p.3; Section II pp.4-5; Section IV p.8
quotes: To ensure a controlled comparison, both models share the same input representation, classical convolutional trunk, average-pooling layer (AvgPool), fully connected layers, and optimizer.
Since each Rot gate contains three rotation angles, the circuit contains 12 trainable rotation parameters in this implementation.
The final dataset contains 1018 nuclei and is randomly split into training and validation sets with a ratio of 4:1.
While the present calculations use noiseless quantum-circuit simulations, future work should examine finite-shot sampling and the resulting stochastic optimization
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup and its limit (noiseless simulation), Sections II and IV.
assertions.reader_inference: No shot noise, hardware noise or hardware run is included, so the gain is a simulation result.

assertions.value: The authors suggest, without testing it separately, that the feature representation of the variational quantum filter is a likely source of the performance difference between the QCNN and the CNN.
quotes: Because the two models differ only in the final filter, this pattern suggests that the feature representation is a likely source of the performance difference.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author interpretation; no ablation is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: A different classical nonlinear filter of similar size was not tested, so the quantum origin of the gain is not isolated.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Recurrent Unit: A Parameter-Efficient Quantum Neural Network Architecture for NISQ Devices
papers.what_it_is: A quantum recurrent neural network design using controlled-SWAP gates and measurement feedforward, tested by simulation on oscillation prediction, WDBC and a 3-versus-5 MNIST task.

assertions.value: The authors report that QRU uses 72 parameters to match a 197-parameter GRU in time series prediction, 35 parameters to reach 96.13% accuracy on WDBC, and 132 parameters to reach 98.05% accuracy on MNIST, against a CNN with approximately 27,265 parameters.
quotes: QRU uses only 72 parameters to match a 197-parameter GRU in time series prediction, 35 parameters to achieve 96.13% accuracy
and 132 parameters to reach 98.05% accuracy, outperforming a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) using approximately 27,265 parameters in MNIST handwritten digit classification
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from simulated experiments on three small tasks.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical comparators are mostly figures taken from other papers, with parameter counts estimated by the authors, and the MNIST task is a single hard digit pair at reduced resolution.

assertions.value: The authors report that over 50 independent runs the 72-parameter QRU had a test mean MSE of 1.94E-02, or 2.49E-03 after outlier removal, and that a GRU needed 197 parameters to reach an MSE of 2.22E-03.
quotes: For comprehensive statistical analysis, we conducted 50 independent experiments for different parameter configurations of each model type.
The original mean MSE in the testing phase was 1.94E-02, which improved to 2.49E-03 after outlier removal
GRU requires expansion to 197 parameters to achieve performance levels close to the 72-parameter QRU (MSE: 2.22E-03)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result on two synthetic oscillation series.
assertions.reader_inference: The QRU figure that matches the GRU is the post-outlier-removal mean, and the unfiltered mean is far higher.

assertions.value: The authors state that all experiments run on classical simulators (PennyLane with a JAX backend), not on quantum hardware, and that the MNIST experiment covers one digit pair chosen as among the hardest to distinguish.
quotes: All experiments use the PennyLane [32] quantum machine learning framework combined with JAX [33] backend.
This pair was chosen in [39] because it is among the hardest digits to distinguish, providing a challenging test scenario for model evaluation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup and scope, Sections 3.1 and 3.4.1.

assertions.value: The authors list as future work a theoretical framework for the quantum state evolution in QRU and validation on physical quantum computers, and note that parameter counts for the classical WDBC baselines are estimated from the original papers.
quotes: Establishing a theoretical framework for quantum state evolution in QRU
Parameter counts are estimated based on architecture descriptions and figures in the original papers.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limits, Section 4.3 and the Table 3.5 note.
